title: Media Mix Modeling for CPG Brands
summary: Manage and view your Scout analyst agent
body_markdown:
Media mix modeling estimates how much each marketing input contributed to sales, using a regression over historical data. For a CPG brand the appeal is obvious: trade spend, retail media, shopper marketing, and brand advertising all compete for the same budget, and nobody can say which one earned its keep.


MMM answers that question, sometimes. This is what it requires, where CPG applications usually fail, and what to do when your data will not support one.


## Key takeaways


- An MMM needs 2 to 3 years of weekly history with genuine variation in each channel. Steady spend produces no signal to fit.
- Price and distribution are the two largest drivers in most CPG models, and leaving them out inflates every media coefficient.
- Correlated channels cannot be separated. If trade and retail media always run together, the model is guessing at the split.
- Below roughly $10M in revenue, a well-run test-and-control read usually beats a model on the same budget.


## What a media mix modeling study actually estimates


The model regresses sales against everything that plausibly moved them: media spend by channel, price, promotion, distribution, seasonality, competitor activity, and a trend term. The output is a coefficient per input, converted into contribution and then into a return figure.


Two refinements make it a marketing model rather than a plain regression. Adstock captures the fact that advertising keeps working after it stops, decaying over weeks. Saturation captures diminishing returns, so the tenth impression is worth less than the first. Both are estimated, and both are places where a modeler's assumptions can quietly drive the answer.


## The data an MMM needs


Input Minimum Why it fails without it


Sales history 104 weeks, ideally 156 Fewer observations than parameters. Seasonality cannot separate from trend.


Media spend by channel by week Actual flighting, not annual totals A flat weekly average has no variation to fit against.


Price and promotion Weekly average retail plus promo flags Price is usually the largest driver. Omit it and media absorbs its effect.


Distribution Weekly store counts or TDP A distribution gain during a campaign is credited to the campaign.


Competitor activity At least category-level promo intensity A competitor's promotion suppresses your sales and reads as your media failing.


The fourth row is the one CPG brands most often skip, and it is the most expensive omission available. A brand that added 74 doors during a campaign and did not include distribution in the model will see a media coefficient carrying the entire distribution effect. The reported return can be several times the truth, and it is the kind of error that gets a budget increased.


## The collinearity problem


Regression cannot separate two inputs that always move together. If your retail media at a given retailer always runs during the same weeks as your trade promotion at that retailer, no amount of modeling can tell you which one drove the lift. The model will still return two coefficients, with confidence intervals wide enough to include almost anything, and those coefficients will be reported to three decimal places in a deck.


This is not a flaw in MMM. It is a fact about the data, and the fix is in the media plan rather than in the model: deliberately stagger channels across weeks or markets so the history contains the variation the model needs. Brands that plan for measurability get better models. Brands that plan for coverage and then commission a model get numbers.


## The sample-size problem for mid-size CPG


A typical CPG MMM fits 15 to 25 parameters. With 104 weekly observations, that is a thin ratio before you account for the fact that weekly sales are autocorrelated, so the effective sample is smaller than the row count implies.


The standard fix is to add cross-sectional variation: model by region or by retailer, which multiplies the observations. That works, and it requires spend data at the same granularity. A brand that buys national media and cannot allocate it regionally does not get this option.


The honest guidance: below roughly $10M in revenue with mostly national media, an MMM will produce results whose error bars are wider than the decisions they inform. Spend the same money on a structured test-and-control read of one channel and you get a cleaner answer to a narrower question, which is usually the better trade.


## What to do instead, or alongside


- Matched-market tests. Hold out comparable regions, run the channel in the others, and read the difference. Slower, far more credible.
- Promotion-level lift measurement against a proper baseline. This handles the largest line in most CPG marketing budgets without any model at all.
- Retailer-level incrementality where the retail media platform supports a holdout. Narrow, but clean.


None of these replace an MMM for the whole-portfolio allocation question. They do answer the specific questions most teams are actually asking, at a fraction of the cost and with error bars you can defend.


## Where Scout fits


Scout is not an MMM platform and does not fit media mix models. What it does is supply and clean the inputs a credible model requires, and measure the largest line in the budget directly. Weekly price, promotion flags, distribution, and store-level velocity come out of your POS and syndicated feeds at a consistent grain, which is the work that usually consumes the first two months of an MMM engagement.


For the trade-spend side of the same question, see[trade promotion effectiveness](https://www.cpgscout.ai/blog/trade-promotion-effectiveness) and[post-promo lift versus baseline](https://www.cpgscout.ai/learn/post-promo-lift-baseline-spins) .


## Frequently asked questions


What is media mix modeling?A statistical method that regresses sales against marketing inputs, price, distribution, seasonality, and competitor activity to estimate how much each contributed. The output is a contribution and return figure per channel.


How much data does an MMM need?At least two years of weekly data, ideally three, with real variation in each channel's spend. Steady weekly spend gives the model nothing to fit, and fewer than 104 observations makes the parameter count untenable.


Is MMM the same as multi-touch attribution?No. MMM is top-down and aggregate, works without user-level tracking, and covers offline channels. Multi-touch attribution is bottom-up and user-level, which makes it a poor fit for CPG where the purchase happens in a store.


Why does my MMM say trade spend has a low return?Often because price is in the model separately. A trade promotion works through price, so a model with both can attribute the effect to the price variable and leave the trade variable looking weak. Check how the two are specified before acting on the result.
